newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma mulls Chechnya, rebels plan polls.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma mulls Chechnya, rebels plan polls.

text.p: Russian lawmakers on Tuesday discussed policy towards rebel Chechnya and separatist leaders announced plans for local elections in a bid to consolidate their control over the southern region.

The State Duma lower house of parliament met behind closed doors to work out its attitude towards the latest peace deal struck between Russian security chief Alexander Lebed and rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov on August 31.

The deal, which ended 21 month of bitter fighting, provided for a withdrawal of troops sent to Chechnya in December 1994 to quell its independence bid, and postponed a decision on the region's future political status for five years.
Rebel leaders said they saw the deal as a victory over Russia, saying it gave Moscow time to find a face-saving way of letting Chechnya go.
But Lebed's bitter opponent, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, told reporters before the Duma hearings started that granting independence to Chechnya was out of question.
Other participants in the hearings said the chamber was not likely to issue any strong statements on the issue.
Lebed and Kulikov, who both addressed the Duma, left without talking to reporters.
"Lebed and Russia have both been forced into such a deal," human rights activist Sergei Kovalyov, who is also a Duma deputy, told reporters in parliament.
The separatists have established control over the whole of Chechnya as Russian troops depart and they are replacing Moscow-installed local authorites with their own ones.

Interfax quoted a source in the Russian General Staff as saying the troop withdrawal from the region would be completed by October 21. It was not clear whether this would include Interior Ministry forces stationed in Chechnya.
Moscow plans to keep two brigades, one from the army and another from the interior ministry, in Chechnya permanently.
Interfax news agency said the rebel leadership, which met in southern Chechnya late on Monday, had decided to hold local elections next January.
The meeting had also finalised the line-up of a coalition government, formed without Moscow's participation, which would include representatives from different Chechen groups.
Itar-Tass news agency later said the polls, which it said might take place in December, would consist of two stages -- elections of a regional parliament and of a new president.
Chechnya's first president, pro-independence Dzhokhar Dudayev, is believed to have been killed earlier this year in a Russian rocket attack.

The rebels do not recognise pro-Moscow Doku Zavgayev, who was elected Chechen president earlier this year in a poll widely criticised as unfair. Zavgayev's government is not taking part in any of the peace negotiations.

Moscow has not officially protested against the separatists' decision to name a coalition government. It was not clear whether Russia, evidently uninvolved in fixing a date for local elections, would recognise their results.
